summary: Jesus warns against giving, praying and fasting to be seen by others, teaches His disciples the Lord’s Prayer, and points them to the Father who sees in secret.
key_insight: Jesus warns against praying to be seen by people, then straight away against praying to be heard “for their many words.” Both turn prayer into a performance, one for an audience and one for God, and both forget that the Father already knows what His children need (6:8).
story: “Take heed that you do not do your charitable deeds before men, to be seen by them.” If they did, Jesus said, they would have no reward from their Father in heaven.

When they gave to the poor, they were not to sound a trumpet as the hypocrites did in the synagogues and in the streets. “Assuredly, I say to you, they have their reward.” Instead, “do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,” and the Father who sees in secret will reward openly.

When they prayed, they were not to stand on the street corners to be seen. “But you, when you pray, go into your room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in the secret place.” Nor were they to pile up empty words like the heathen, who think they will be heard for their many words. “For your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him.”

“In this manner, therefore, pray: Our Father in heaven, Hallowed be Your name.” The prayer asks for His kingdom to come and His will to be done on earth as in heaven, for daily bread, for forgiveness as we forgive our debtors, not to be led into temptation, and for deliverance from the evil one. Jesus then underlined one line: if they forgave others, the Father would forgive them; if they did not, neither would the Father forgive them.

When they fasted, they were not to look gloomy and disfigure their faces so that people would notice. “But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,” so that only the Father who sees in secret would know, and He would reward them openly.

scene.label: Sounding a trumpet
scene.text: No record shows anyone literally blowing a trumpet to announce a gift. Jesus may be using a vivid picture of self-advertising, or pointing to the thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests in the temple courts, into which worshipers dropped their coins.

scene.label: Your room
scene.text: The word Jesus uses means an inner storeroom. In a simple house it was probably the only room with a door that shut. Prayer there had no audience but God.

scene.label: Debts
scene.text: In Aramaic, the language Jesus probably spoke, a common word for sin also meant a debt. Luke’s form of the prayer puts both ideas side by side: “forgive us our sins, For we also forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (Luke 11:4).

scene.label: Fasting
scene.text: The Law required one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Devout Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). Fasters often left their hair unwashed and put ashes on their heads, which made a fast easy to notice.

scene.label: The closing words
scene.text: The NKJV includes the prayer’s last line, “For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen,” and notes that some of the oldest manuscripts do not have it. Its words echo David’s praise in 1 Chronicles 29:11.

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew records this section, a warning aimed at religious people rather than irreligious ones. Luke gives the Lord’s Prayer on another occasion, when a disciple asked, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1–4). Matthew sets the prayer near the center of the sermon, framed by warnings against religion done for show.

seeing.reveals: Jesus knows God as the Father “who sees in secret,” and He invites His disciples to pray “Our Father” with Him. He opens to them His own way of relating to God.
seeing.living: Keep some of your giving and praying where only the Father sees, and let it stay there. And when you pray “forgive us our debts,” name before Him the person you need to forgive.
seeing.ponder: If no one ever knew about your prayers or your giving, would you still do them the same way?

preaching.big_idea: Seek the Father’s reward, not the crowd’s, for He sees in secret.
outline: The principle: not to be seen (1)
preaching.watch_for: Each practice follows the same pattern: do not be like the hypocrites; “they have their reward”; but the Father “who sees in secret will reward you openly.” The Lord’s Prayer breaks the pattern and stands at the center.

title: Giving, Praying and Fasting in Secret
